text: Constrained Route Planning for a Simulated Hexapod
Jin Wayne Foo,  Juo Wei Lai1, Latifah Mohammed Abdulrahman1, Gulhajar Melebayeva1, Wen Zer Goo1, Anfel Fodil1, Tiong Yew Tang1

Research Center for Human Machine Collaboration (HUMAC), Faculty of Engineering and Technology, Sunway University No. 5, Jalan Universiti, Bandar Sunway, 47500 Selangor Darul, Ehsan, Malaysia.waynejinfoo123@gmail.com, tiongyewt@sunway.edu.my

In this work we assess landmark search and final local modification in body-route planning for a simulated hexapod. Obstacle-clearance, deadline, nominal battery and terrain-exposure constraints are shared by six configurations. Parameter selection includes 64 trials and 8 development maps, the main test includes 576 trials and 32 maps, resulting in 640 planning trials. The complete planner, Constrained Landmark Route Planning (CLRP) achieves acceptance of 93/96 main-test attempts as compared to 94/96 for coordinate-based particle swarm optimization (PSO-C) and 90/96 for the planner without final adjustment. Removing landmark search retains 93 acceptances and reduces mean search time from 0.376 to 0.196 s. Complete CLRP has a conditional mean paired-map relative score improvement of 0.924% over this reduced version. The mean paired-map relative score improvement against PSO-C is 0.690%, the zero median and the descriptive 95 % bootstrap interval is [−0.255, 2.312] %. This statistical interval contains zero and does not demonstrate a mean score advantage. A separate diagnostic comprises 16 executions: four missions under four assistance conditions. Full and half-scale assistance each finish all four missions. Both zero-assistance conditions complete none and time out at 180 s. Assisted executions have no detected foot contact under the six-foot criterion. Results quantify the planning tradeoffs and dependence on direct body assistance. The nominal battery costs are model outputs which are not physically or electrically validated.
Keywords: Hexapod; planning; optimization; simulation; reproducibility

The movement path of a robot should not have obstacles and meet the conditions of the task. Even a short route can miss its deadline or leave insufficient battery reserve to reach a charging station. The current model considers walking speed in different terrain, time of turns and nominal battery use, and exposure to difficult terrain. These costs must be taken into consideration when selecting the route, and should be determined separately whether all the task requirements are met. In this work, we want to examine how landmark search and the resulting final local route refinement during planning affects acceptance, route score and computation in MuJoCo [1] whilst controlling for map, evaluator and task constraints. The complete planner (CLRP) features initial corridor search, more links around obstacles and terrain boundaries, and local refinement of intermediate route coordinates. The two particle swarm and ant-inspired planners which select the points from the initial routes, the particle swarm planner which modifies the coordinates of the intermediate points, and the two versions of CLRP with the elimination of one search stage are analyzed. The experiment is not intended to provide a new swarm update rule but to assess the configurations used. The study contrasts between three goals: accepting with resource limitation, differences in scores of accepted attempts for both approaches, and the number of computations required to determine routes. Eight development maps are used to pick configurations prior to the major evaluation on 32 maps with three paired repetitions. Stage-removal comparisons are used to determine if adding more search will make an accepted route better or change the level of acceptance. There are four separate maps that investigate dependence on direct body support, separating route acceptance from locomotion validation. The assumptions of walking speed and turning, along with the two-dimensional body-clearance envelope depend on the hexapod application. The map and pose are given directly to the planner which then plans body trajectories and not complete sequences of foot placements. The results are for the geometry and nominal resource model specified. This is a consistent framework to evaluate the planning stages. Battery cost and assisted movement is not a measurement of physical robot performance.

A* uses the sum of the cost incurred to reach a point and a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost [2]. The particle swarm optimization updates the candidate solutions by using particle motion and the best position of each particle and the swarm [3]. The ant system bases on pheromone and heuristic information to guide route construction [4]. A visibility graph is a graph that links points by straight line segments that are unobstructed [5]. The initial search, population updates and graph connections employed here are based on these proven methods. The best candidate found by the constrained search is not guaranteed to be the best candidate in the world. Under resource constraints, routing is more than just minimizing the length one route. Ma combines A* and label setting for multimodal routes with consideration for resources and mode-sequences [6]. Although the transportation model describes related constrained search techniques, the network and mode-chain problems considered here are different than the planar robot paths. The current approach is based on an initial search label set and a set of landmark candidates to which continuous point refinement is applied. Deadlines, nominal battery allowances for outbound and inbound legs and terrain exposure are evaluated by one evaluator. A hybrid approach between particle swarm optimization and control-barrier-function velocity adjustments for mobile-robot trajectory planning is proposed by Guo et al. [7]. They have a safety feature that is linked to planning and controlling speed. The current comparison keeps the segment-clearance test, and compares acceptance and score in the same resource constraints. Does not make use of or test their controller. Modification of the collision model, of the way of initialisation or execution influences both the comparison and the optimizer. Hexapod research also concerns motion lower than the body-route. On LittleStrong [8] Yin et al. optimize swing trajectories, gait timing and gait sequence. In simulation and experiments, Chen et al. incorporate terrain characteristics and the cost of traversal, foot placement and locomotion strategy [9]. The current work fixes the gait controller and provides the terrain data as input and also examines the elimination of body-route planning stages. This separate assistance diagnostic is not meant to be a substitute for the physical and foot-placement assessments of those studies. These studies motivate the idea of a specific experimental question: how do acceptance and route score vary when landmark search and final adjustment are combined under a single evaluator? Complete configurations are compared as the way they are initialized and how they represent routes are different. They are not copies of each of the referenced planners. The research records these and numbers both route evaluations as well as geometric queries, as per the COCO procedure emphasis on initialization, parameter selection and termination criteria [10]. The comparison is for the implementations and the resource model mentioned.

The robot model has six legs with each leg having three articulated joints. The total mass of the imported model is 97.52 kg and its base mass is 35 kg. The total mass of the assembled MuJoCo model is 113.32 kg including the mass of the base 46 kg. It comes with wheels and a scanner, for a total of 23 actuators. All experiments use walking mode; the wheels and scanner are still considered as part of the simulated mass. The MuJoCo robot is shown in the walking configuration in Fig. 1, in a static snapshot. The perspective is stationary, allowing to see the assembly with the wheels and scanner. Close objects are removed from view. This planning is based on the maps and task constraints from Section 5 and is reflected in the results in Section 6.
Figure 1. Static view of the simulated hexapod in its walking configuration. The wheels and scanner remain part of the assembly.

The imported robot spec says that leg-joint torque limits are 60 Nm and angular velocity limits are 20 rad/s. These are specified as limits in the specification. No physical measurements of motor torque-speed characteristics, battery depletion or robot mass. The assembled simulation is the one which is evaluated here, while the imported values for the masses differentiate between source model and assembled model. MuJoCo takes 0.004 s steps in advancing the physics. The motion controller uses a period of 0.016 s, or every four physics steps. The acceleration due to gravity is 9.81 m/s². Gravity compensation is on by default on 18 leg bodies. Gravity compensation and direct body assistance are two distinct mechanisms: the gravity compensation acts on the selected bodies to remove the effect of gravity, and the direct body assistance acts on the velocity of the free body. Body assistance limits the vertical velocity and roll/pitch rates once per controller frame. Also modifies horizontal velocity and yaw-rate per physics step. At assistance scale 1 the horizontal velocity is set equal to the requested velocity. At scale 0.5, each correction will keep 50% of the current velocity and add 50% of the requested velocity. This mixture is used 4 times in each controller frame. At scale 0, these direct body-velocity corrections are disabled. The scale is for velocity blending and not for a support force. Ground truth position, heading, obstacle geometry and terrain information is directly accessed from the simulator and passed to the planner. These inputs are not based on measurement from the sensors. Each method has the same starting point, starting orientation, destination and estimated time of return to charging station. Comparisons of the route choice choices are thus on the same known map. Not including sensor noise, localization errors and map reconstruction.

A path P is an ordered sequence of points that lie on the horizontal plane. The first and last points are the given starting and ending. Each point is connected by a straight segment, in order. The spacing of the first search grid is 0.25 m and the directions of the motion are eight. Diagonal movement is not allowed at blocked grid corners. All returned segments will have to undergo the same clearance test with the planar obstacle geometry. The radius of the robot is defined as 1.82 m, tracking margin is 0.12 m and the tolerance of segment clearance is 0.005 m. These values are used for planning clearance model. The analysis assumes a trajectory for the robot body and does not generate three dimensional foot-placement trajectories. The terrain map is used to specify areas having varying walking-speed and difficulty values. Terrain difficulty at each grid location is determined by equations (1) and (2).

The clip function maps the intermediate value g to the final difficulty d in [0, 2]. The variables s, h and u represent slope (in radians), height range (in meters) and the standard deviation of the sampled ground heights (in meters) of the population, respectively, and f represents the semantic softness. The heights are sampled in nine locations with offsets of −1.82, 0 and 1.82 m on each horizontal axis. Slope is the arctangent of the gradient magnitude of the footprint-averaged sampled height field on the 0.25 m grid. The values of f for the various terrain grades tested (grades 0, 1, 2) are 0, 0.25, and 0.60, respectively. Terrain-grade requests are made with a 1.1 m buffer around patch boundaries. Difficulty is sampled at intervals no greater than 0.125 m along each route segment. The difficulty for each route sample is the one of the closest grid cell. Segment exposure = length of segment x the mean sampled difficulty. The sum of segment exposures is the total exposure R. This amount is based on a terrain map and does not reflect an estimate of slip likelihood.

The route evaluator returns distance D in meters, estimated travel time T in seconds, nominal battery use E in percentage points and terrain exposure R. First heading is π/2 radians. Predicted time assumes that travel is at terrain-dependent speed limits, headings change at 1 rad/s, and there is an acceleration allowance. For terrain grades 0, 1 and 2, the speed limits are 0.75, 0.65 and 0.38 m/s, respectively. The four quantities are combined together in a score Q in equation (3) lower values of Q are better. The denominators represent one score unit in terms of 50 m of distance, 90 s of predicted time, 30 nominal battery percentage points or 80 exposure units. These fixed trade-offs were not based on robot measurements or optimized to the results of the main-test.

Acceptance" means that the predicted time of arrival is within the deadline, the exposure is within the terrain limit, and the required nominal battery allowance is within the battery available. The required allowance is given by equation (4). Subscript return represents the nominal battery consumption of a route from the destination to a charging station. The fixed reserve requirements are the 1.25 multiplier and the additional six percentage points.

The battery cost model is defined as 0.70 percentage points per walking meter and 0.015 per second, 0.08 per turning radian and a 0.10 start/stop allowance. These coefficients have not been adjusted to electrical measurements. The four score terms are not independent physical outcomes since distance, travel time and turning also contribute to E. When they are combined they reflect a fixed preference of these route properties. The six-point reserve gives an allowance and the 1.25 multiplier applies to the outward-and-return cost. Both rules are not statistically calibrated probability of accomplishing a physical mission. The same parameters are used for all evaluations. No sensitivity testing is done for different score weights or reserve settings. In this paper, battery use refers to the output of this equation-based model. The route score is not a conversion from mechanical to electrical battery work. The charging station and return path are predetermined at the start of each trial prior to comparing planners. In turn, the planners choose an outward path to follow, within the same limitation. The destination deadline is for the outward leg. Outward and return routes are included in the motion experiment, as well as eight seconds of simulated station service included in the completed mission times. Whole-mission distance and elapsed time refer to the execution of destination and return task, while D and T refer to the planned outward route. Unfinished executions may stop at either leg. The candidate ranking process first determines if routes meet all constraints, and then if they do not. All constraint raw excesses at most 10⁻⁸ are considered to be zero. Larger positive excesses are divided by their corresponding limits and summed. The lowest total normalized violation factor is ranked first, and if total normalized violations are equal, the lowest Q is ranked first. Lower Q is the highest priority of routes accepted. A rejected candidate will not replace an accepted route.

There are three stages of CLRP. The first investigates initial corridors in the context of time, battery and terrain constraints. A corridor is a first-passage through free space that serves as a path from which alternatives are developed in later stages. The second stage involves the addition of connections through points around the obstacles and terrain boundaries. Final stage is route adaptation with the removal of internal points, point shift towards their projections on adjacent segments, replacement of points by midpoints and shift of point coordinates. The highest ranked route is kept for the entire search and only changed when the rank of a candidate improves. Routes must meet the common segment-clearance test prior to costing. Route geometries that are repeated re-use cached evaluations. The same rules do also apply to the last local-adjustment stage of the planners that have been evaluated. The time fractions of CLRP, landmark cap, size of local moves and the parameters for initial searches are represented in Table 1. These settings restrict what is taken into account during a trial. Graph connection and a full route evaluation are performed separately. Before a line segment is added to a finished route, it is possible for graph search to discard it. Alternatives with varying resource costs and heading are also left over for graph search. Local-adjustment stage – alters an entire series of route points. A common limit on full route evaluations does not imply equal numbers of geometric queries. The entire CLRP process is outlined in Algorithm 1. All the stages are evaluated by the same evaluator and the same ranking rule. Route evaluations during initialization count toward the fixed common ceiling. Algorithm 1.

Search for routes on CLRP. Inputs: known obstacle geometry, terrain, start, destination, and initial heading, task constraints, fixed return allowance, random seed, and 2 s search-time limit, 240-route-evaluation limit, and 40,000-expansion limit.
1. Perform the first (resource-aware) refiner for up to 40% of the nominal search time. Use the common limit for its route assessments and keep its best available route. If budget allows

2. Test the direct start to destination route. Ignore bad or rejected geometry. Use common metrics and constraint-ranking rule to evaluate only valid routes, reusing cached evaluations for repeated geometry.

3. Gather internal points of the initial route, inflated obstacle corners and points around terrain boundaries. Eliminate out-of-bounds and blocked points and duplicate points. Order the rest of the candidates by the sum of their distances to the start and destination. Keep a maximum of 44 points, including the start and destination.

4. Construct collision free visibility links. Explore the resulting graph with heading-aware states, in turn by score, time and battery. Do not exceed 40,000 (minus expansions used by the initial refiner) and 32% nominal time for this stage. Use common ranking rule to evaluate full routes.

5. Test the best retained route with internal-point deletion, movement halfway towards the neighbouring-segment projection, midpoint replacement as well as moves in eight directions at step size of 0.75, 0.25 and 0.08 m. Keep only improvements in rank. At every step size, terminate after 3 passes (or no improvement pass or shared budget is exhausted).
Output the best route retained and metrics, or initial search status if no route is retained. Rejected routes are never the first ones used when compared to accepted routes.

PSO-P and ACO-P choose subsequences of points from the initial corridors, and carry out the common final local-adjustment stage. The parameters, for population sizes, update coefficients and iteration limits, are listed in table 1. The internal path points of PSO-C are represented by continuous coordinates. It begins by performing the same configured initial corridor search as CLRP. The longest segments are divided in half until there are at least 6 interior points in the path. Corners are maintained in the subdivision. The start and end points do not change. When swarm search occurs the particle representation does not change; it has the same number of internal points, with x and y coordinates that can vary within the map. Each particle is randomly given Gaussian perturbations of the internal point coordinates (apart from the first particle), with a standard deviation of 2 m. Each coordinate change in the swarm iterations is capped at ±2 m. The range of the particle positions on the horizontal axes is limited to [−24, 24] m (Table 1). Proposals that don't pass the clearance test are denied. If particle proposals do not enhance the initial best route, then the initial best route is available, and the final adjustment shares the common evaluation ceiling. The route representations and initial-route procedures are different between PSO-C and PSO-P. The evaluation is done to assess the total impact of these decisions in implementation. Does not only focus on the impact of representation. The results reported are for the set route objective and configuration.
4.3 Elimination of planning stages and search limits

CLRP noL is without landmark search, and CLRP noP is without final local adjustment, or polishing. The selected CLRP settings for the stages that are retained are also carried over to both variants. In particular, noP discards the last adjustment and preserves the operations in the first refiner. These comparisons are made to assess the impact if one stage is taken off the selected planner. The down-tuned variants will not be re-tuned on the primary-test maps. The chosen search parameters are shown in table 1. Table 1. Selected search settings: noL omits landmark search; noP omits final adjustment.

16 particles; 40 iterations/corridor; inertia 0.72; coefficients 1.49; velocity clip 0.25

Each method is given a search-time limit of 2 s and a limit of 240 collision-free routes evaluated. Route evaluations during method initialization are also part of this total. Rejected proposals are collision checked (not complete route) and the result counts as a geometric query. A method may stop below both limits when its search procedures end. PSO-C may take up the evaluation limit before time limit. The wall timer contains initialization and refinement for the particular method. Shared map preparation takes place prior to the methods running, and involves preparations of the scenes, construction of common graphs, return-route preparation and calculation of destination-based lower bounds. Reported search time thus includes only some planning by all methods, and excludes preparation common to all methods for a given case.

The study uses eight development maps with seeds from 2130000 to 2130007 and 32 main-test maps with seeds from 2140000 to 2140031. The map types alternate between open, cluttered, rough and corridor. There are two development maps and eight main-test maps for each category. The horizontal range of each map is from −24 to 24 m. Open, Cluttered, Rough and Corridor maps have 5, 16, 7 and 4 generated obstacles respectively. There are also two interrupted barriers on the corridor maps. The four families of maps have 1, 2, 4 and 3 terrain patches, respectively. Obstacles, shallow terrain tiles and areas which affect walking speed and exposure are defined by each map. The same geometry and terrain is given to all six planners for a specific case. Start and destination proposals are sampled between −17 and 17 m (with a starting distance of 12–26 m) on each axis. Proposals are moved to free grid locations and kept if their eventual separation is ≥ 10 m. Deadlines are 45, 70, 110 and 160 s. Available nominal battery levels are 45%, 65%, 85% and 100%, and exposure limits are 10, 20 and 40. The overall distance to the charging station is determined in advance prior to comparing the different methods. The nominal battery cost coefficients are the same for all maps. Changing battery allowances changes the available resource limit and not the nominal battery use assigned to a meter or a turn. The experiment modifies the geometry of the maps and task constraints. It does not measure a variety of physical battery characteristics.

Two parameter profiles are used for each of the four base methods and tested on the development maps. The profile that has more accepted attempts gets picked first. When acceptance counts are equal, the profile with the lowest mean score among accepted attempts is chosen. The default profile is used for Exact ties. All of the base methods use the default, and both reduced forms of the CLRP do the same. The other PSO-P configuration consists of 24 particles, inertia of 0.55, and social/cognitive values of 1.3 and 1.7. The alternative ACO-P configuration consists of 18 ants, an evaporation rate of 0.35 and a heuristic exponent of 3. The alternative PSO-C profile consists of 20 particles, 60 iterations, inertia of 0.75, cognitive and social coefficients of 1.6 and a perturbation and velocity bound of 4 m. The alternative CLRP profile consists of a combination of initial-search fraction of 0.55, extra-point fraction of 0.25, 60 points, 12 labels per state, and local move sizes of 0.50, 0.15 and 0.05 m. All other settings are unchanged from their respective default settings. The development phase includes 64 planning attempts (8 maps, 4 methods and 2 profiles). The main test has 576 shots: 32 maps, 6 methods and 3 repetitions for each method. Thus there are 96 main-test attempts each method and 640 for the whole experiment. Before the results of the main tests, maps, parameter-selection criteria, and primary analysis were set. No external preregistration was done. All scheduled attempts were included in the acceptance count, including all main-test attempts. The three repetitions of each map have the same geometry and task constraints and quantify algorithmic variation within each map. These are NOT three separate maps. These differences in relative score are averaged across all repetitions where they are mutually accepted in each map and then summarized across all maps. Thus the number of mutual accepted repetitions is not considered as weight when using a paired map.

Only attempts in which a route is accepted by both the CLRP and comparison method are compared. Attempts accepted by only one method and attempts rejected by both methods are counted separately. The relative score difference for a paired attempt is defined by equation (5). Qc is the score for the comparison method and Qv is the score of CLRP. Positive difference indicates that CLRP has the lower score; negative difference indicates that the comparison method has the lower score. Ties are absolute differences between Qc and Qv of at most 10⁻⁸.

The reported mean and median summarize the within-map averages of paired relative score differences. Descriptive 95% percentile bootstrap intervals are based on 5,000 resamples of maps with random seed 41104, following the resampling principle in [11]. The repetitions are still in the same map. The intervals are subject to acceptance by both methods and are not adjusted for the five comparisons. A relative-improvement threshold is used only for descriptive purposes of counting larger improvements: 0.5%. Map-family breakdowns, computational summaries and map-by-map displays and omission analyses were performed following the main test. They record results without altering the set-up or main-test sample. One paired map is omitted at a time in the omission analysis and the mean is calculated. The resulting means show each omitted map's influence on the overall mean. All maps are used in the main analysis. Evaluations run on Linux with Python 3.10.12, MuJoCo 3.9.0, NumPy 2.2.6 and SciPy 1.15.3. The processor is an Intel Core i5-7600, 3.50 GHz and 4 logical processors. Many processes are executed at the same time on the desktop. This shared-desktop configuration is reported in recorded wall times, and is not exclusive processor usage or deployment latency.

The four maps used in the motion experiment have seeds 1670000 to 1670003. Each mission takes the CLRP path on the first repetition of the map and the set path back to a charging station. Outward route lengths are 21.36, 22.30, 23.45 and 19.78 m, respectively. The initial nominal battery levels are 45%, 85%, 45% and 100% respectively. The first-repetition routes are a stand-alone diagnostic to the 32 main-test maps. This is done in four conditions: full body with gravity compensation, half scale with gravity compensation, zero with gravity compensation and zero without gravity compensation. The same path tracker is used for all conditions and a maximum simulated execution time of 180 s. Completion is defined as getting to the destination and back to the station. Unfinished missions time out at 180 s, a time limit that is different from the planner's outward-route time limit. Mission times are completed and includes eight seconds of simulated station service. Gravity compensation is checked once the locomotion controller has been initialized. The no-compensation condition makes all the leg-body compensation values zero at that point. Four initial executions where the compensation was restored by the initialization were not included and rerun once the removal was verified. The final comparison consists of 16 executions: four missions under each of four conditions. These are routes that have been evaluated and are not a new test set for locomotion, but rather a diagnostic of the execution model. Foot contact is recorded for each Physics step (0.004 s). Contacts with external geometries are reported if the contact distance is 0.002 m or less, with each of the six foot geometries being considered as contacting an external geometry. Mean contact feet = average number of feet found in contact per sample. No contact fraction is the fraction of samples in which there are no foot contacts found. Only the six feet of the detector count, contacts with other parts of the robot do not count. Body tilt is derived from the body orientation. Low tilt describes the assisted controller's behavior; roll and pitch angular velocities are directly adjusted using orientation feedback. Positive actuator work is determined by multiplying the actuator force by the actuator velocity, keeping only positive power, integrating over time and summing over actuators. It does not consider work added by direct modification of body velocity. These metrics characterize motion and actuator effort of the model as it moves under the given assistance condition.

There are no trial error logs in any of the 640 planning attempts. The default profile for each base method is selected by development. The main-test acceptance counts and mean search times are shown in Table 2. CLRP, PSO-P, ACO-P and CLRP noL each accept 93 of 96 attempts, while PSO-C gets 94 and CLRP noP gets 90. All 20 rejected main-test attempts exceed the predicted outbound deadline; their battery and terrain-exposure checks pass.
Table 2. Accepted main-test routes and mean search time.

Against PSO-C, CLRP has 33 lower-score paired accepted attempts, 27 ties and 33 higher-score attempts. PSO-C alone accepts one attempt; CLRP alone accepts none, and both reject two. The mean paired-map relative score improvement is 0.690%, the median is zero, and the descriptive 95% bootstrap interval is [−0.255, 2.312]%. The interval includes zero.

Table 3 shows the means and intervals for all five comparisons. The CLRP-versus-PSO-P and CLRP-versus-ACO-P comparisons both have zero medians. Compared with CLRP noL, complete CLRP has 27 lower-score paired accepted attempts, 57 ties and nine higher-score attempts. Compared with CLRP noP, complete CLRP has 57 lower-score attempts, 33 ties, no higher-score attempts and three attempts accepted only by complete CLRP. The scoring and acceptance effects of each removed stage are separate results.
Table 3. Paired score differences favoring CLRP; n is the number of paired maps.

Table 2 includes all 96 trials for each method. The map-level analysis in Table 3 considers only mutually accepted attempts averaged within each map. The comparison with CLRP noP consists of 30 paired maps; the other comparisons comprise 31 paired maps. Conditional score comparisons do not replace the acceptance results for the full sample.

All resource rejections occur on corridor maps. All methods accept 24 of 24 attempts in each of the open, cluttered and rough families. Corridor acceptance is 21 of 24 for CLRP, PSO-P, ACO-P and CLRP noL; 22 of 24 for PSO-C; and 18 of 24 for CLRP noP. There are eight maps per family each repeated three times. These counts identify the extra PSO-C acceptances and the three acceptances that are not there when final adjustment is eliminated. Search effort for all 96 search efforts for each method is reported in Table 4. In 84/96 attempts, PSO-C achieves the 240-route evaluation limit, while no other method achieves this limit. The median number of route-evaluation counts is 33 for CLRP and 21 with landmark search disabled. Median geometric-clearance query count is 1,033 for CLRP, 2,142.5 for PSO-C and 146.5 for CLRP noL. The shared map preparation time is 0.715 s (median) and 0.895 s (maximum) and is not accounted for in the individual search timers. While a route evaluation provides metrics for the entire route, a clearance query may reject a segment prior to evaluating the entire route. Table 4 summarizes search work over 96 attempts per method; evaluations count complete collision-free routes.
Table 4. Search work over 96 attempts; evaluations count complete collision-free routes.

All searches are completed in 2 s or less. Common route-evaluation limits do not imply equal search effort: the PSO-C configuration reaches the limit in most searches, while others terminate at a lower count. These elapsed times are for the shared-desktop use case described in Section 5.3, and do not include shared preparation time.

All 31 relative score improvements achieved with paired-maps are shown in figure 2, from minus 1.718% to plus 23.202%. The highest gain is on Map 24. The full 31-map mean is 0.690%; omitting Map 24 gives −0.060% over the remaining 30 maps. For the noP comparison, it is leave-one-map-out, remain positive, ranging from 0.682% to 0.822%. These post hoc summaries are computed as influence within the unchanged primary sample.
Figure 2. Average over jointly accepted repetitions of the CLRP score difference against PSO-C on each paired map. Positive values favor CLRP. All points remain in the primary mean.

Map 24 is still in the main dataset that the mean and bootstrap interval is computed from. This map drives the positive mean, which coexists with a zero map-level median and equal attempt-level lower- and higher-score counts against PSO-C. Omission calculation is a measure of concentration of the result. It is not sufficient to warrant the exclusion of the map from the main analysis.

All three repetitions are acceptable for both methods. In the CLRP, the route is repeated the same distance in each repetition, 20.803 m, and score 1.310. PSO-C has a mean distance of 27.135 m and a mean score of 1.706. CLRP's predicted time, nominal battery cost and exposure are 32.959 s, 15.446 percentage points and 1.012, respectively, compared to PSO-C means of 42.584 s, 20.066 percentage points and 1.665. CLRP scores are lower in all four components for each paired repetition. Repetition zero is shown in Figure 3. PSO-C goes down a longer road to the west. This is why you are seeing the scores of the returned routes vary, but it does not specify one particular internal factor in the optimizer.

Figure 3. Routes on corridor map 24, repetition 0. The circle and star are the start and finish points. The black squares are obstacles; amber is terrain. This example is chosen post hoc because it has the largest positive paired-map effect.

This example was chosen following the main analysis as it has the most powerful paired-map effect with PSO-C and it is positive. It is a one instance in Figure 2 and is not a typical improvement. Complete distribution and the zero median are also necessary for the interpretation of the comparison.

Full and half-scale assistance each finish all four missions. All unfulfilled missions will time-out after 180 s under both zero-assistance conditions. Table 5 shows a mixing of the completion and foot contact measures for the 16 valid executions, of which eight complete. GC refers to leg-body gravity compensation. Each contact range is a summary of four missions: mean feet is the average number of feet detected in contact per physics sample, no-contact percentage is percentage of physics samples without detected foot contacts. The detector does not count contacts with other parts of the robot.
Table 5. Completion and foot-contact ranges across four missions per condition.

Full-assistance mission distances are between 34.71 and 42.83 m, while times are between 62.85 and 89.63 s. Half-scale distances range from 34.75 to 42.91 m and times from 62.83 to 89.66 s. Completed mission times include 8 seconds of station service. Under zero direct assistance, traveled distances at timeout are 0.324 to 0.326 m with leg-body gravity compensation and 0.376 to 0.381 m without it. Maximum assisted body tilt is less than 0.410 degrees and roll and pitch angular velocities are controlled directly with orientation feedback. None of the eight assisted executions show any foot contacts on any of the sampled physics steps during the 6-foot contact test. These results demonstrate route following with direct body assistance and do not validate propulsion via foot–ground interaction. Under zero direct assistance, small horizontal displacements occur, but none of the four missions completes within 180 s, with leg-body gravity compensation either enabled or verified disabled. These results refer to the four missions tested, and are not an estimate of a general hardware failure rate.

Under the tested settings final local adjustment is more accepted and gives lower scores in more accepted attempts than landmark search. Removing it loses three acceptances, all repetitions of one corridor map (seed 2140011), while removing landmark search results in a loss of recorded computation and no loss of acceptance. The retained route cannot worsen in rank within a run because only rank-improving modifications are kept. The empirical result is a quantitative estimation of the trade-offs at the chosen settings. Separately-timed stage-removal trials do not ensure the same history of searches across repetitions. Initialization quality can be separated from the contribution of later stages using an initial-route-only baseline and a matched-budget comparison, both of which are not included here. The study does not demonstrate a mean paired-map relative score advantage for CLRP over PSO-C. The mean paired-map relative score improvement is 0.690%, the descriptive 95% bootstrap interval contains zero and the median is zero. When the interval contains zero, it doesn't mean equality or inferiority. PSO-C accepts one additional scheduled attempt and map 24 has significant impact on the positive mean relative improvement. The mean relative improvements for the two comparisons (CLRP-versus-PSO-P and CLRP-versus-ACO-P) are positive, and the median paired-map effects are 0, for the configurations tested. The different ways of initialization and the different ways of representation make it impossible to credit representation by itself. The five intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons, and are not confirmation evidence. For all methods, every tested non-corridor action is accepted and therefore, differences in acceptance are limited to corridor actions in the four map families. The 3 repetitions indicate the amount of algorithmic variation within the map(s) and do not produce a number of independent main-test maps greater than 32. A separate evaluation is required for more complex or unknown environs. There is no sensitivity evaluation of the score weights and reserve settings. There's an overlap of route preferences within the combined score, since distance and duration are also factors in battery usage. There is no physical battery savings verified by electrical measurements and the work done by direct body assistance is not included in the work done by the actuators. Search times are not deployment latency measurements, but are recorded in the shared-desktop configuration, not shared-preparation. The motion diagnostic defines dependence on direct body assistance to the four missions tested. Completed missions and low tilt do not necessarily prove a walking gait, as assistance is required to correct body velocities and roll/pitch rates. That interpretation is further curtailed by the six foot contact measurements. The scope of the simulation is defined by known map and pose inputs, various source and assembled masses, and the lack of physical motor, battery, terrain and contact measurements. The ability to physically walk and sense based navigation is not assessed.

Final local refinement improves acceptance from 90 to 93 out of 96 attempts on 32 main-test maps; the three additional acceptances are repetitions of one corridor map. In contrast, landmark search leaves acceptance unchanged at 93 of 96 and provides a conditional mean paired-map relative score improvement of 0.924% when compared to its removal, with a mean search time of 0.196 s without the landmarks and 0.376 s with the landmarks. This is because the two stage-removal comparisons exhibit different acceptance-score/computation trade-offs. There is no mean score advantage shown over PSO-C: the mean paired-map relative improvement is 0.690%, the median is 0, and the description 95% bootstrap interval contains 0. PSO-C accepts one additional scheduled attempt. There are 16 valid motion executions in a separate diagnostic. Full-scale and half-scale assistance each complete all four missions. Both zero-assistance conditions complete none and time out at 180 s, with leg-body gravity compensation enabled or verified disabled. Under the defined 6-foot test, all assisted executions show no foot contact. The study thus separates the acceptance of a limited body route from the validation of an unassisted locomotion of the body. The costs and tradeoffs reported are for the particular simulation and objective.
